questions.stem: A 35-year-old man complained of new onset numbness around his mouth and face. He had been started on colistin (2.5 mg/kg ideal body weight IV q12 hours) 3 days earlier for a urinary tract infection and had clinically responded. He was paraplegic and had a long-term Foley catheter. He had no known drug allergies. On examination, there were no appreciable lesions around his mouth. He was afebrile. Investigations: Total white cell count 10.1 ×109/L (admission WCC 13.2 ×109/L) Serum creatinine 0.45 mg/dL (baseline serum creatinine = 0.4 mg/dL) Admission urinalysis: 50 white blood cells/high power field; >105CFU Klebsiella pneumoniae, resistant to meropenem, sensitive to colistin. K. pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC) detected
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Switch colistin to ceftazidime–avibactam IV The patient is likely experiencing colistin-induced neurotoxicity, warranting discontinuation of colistin. Ceftazidime–avibactam is active against KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and would be an appropriate agent to switch to. Ceftriaxone would not be expected to provide coverage of KPC-producing Enterobacteriaceae strains. Ceftolozane–tazobactam does not provide activity against KPC-producing strains. Discontinuing therapy for a complicated urinary tract infection at day 3 of therapy is not appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q3

questions.question: Colistin is protein bound in a nonlinear way: at low concentrations a small amount is protein bound, and at high concentrations a large amount is protein bound.
questions.question_raw: Colistin is protein bound, but in a nonlinear way.  At low concentrations, a small amount is protein bound.  At high concentrations, a large amount is protein bound.

parts.text: What effect does protein binding have on drug activity?
What must you measure in order to appropriately use this drug?

parts_raw.text: What effect does protein binding have on drug activity?
b) What must up you measure in order to appropriately use this drug?

questions.model_answer: a) Only the free (unbound) fraction of colistin is microbiologically active, so protein binding lowers the effective active concentration and must be built into the PK/PD target: with ~50% protein binding a free AUC/MIC of ~12 corresponds to a total AUC/MIC of ~24, which underlies the target average steady-state concentration of 2 µg/mL. b) Renal function (creatinine clearance), body weight, and the plasma colistin concentration (therapeutic drug monitoring against a target average steady-state concentration of ~2 µg/mL). c) (1) Dose-related nephrotoxicity (RIFLE-defined AKI in ~30-60%). (2) Dose-related neurotoxicity/neuromuscular blockade (muscle weakness, apnea; potentiated by aminoglycosides).

cohort_answer.text:
It affects the efficiency of the drug, if it's protein bound, it cannot enter tissue/cells/ exert it's pharmacologic effect. Bound drug has a slower release over time. Cannot clear it as easily.
MOA: enter the outer membrane and interact electrostatically with the phospholipids in the membranes, thereby disrupting the membrane by competitive displacement of divalent cations. Also bind to LPS and block the effects of endotoxin.
AMR: changes to LPS by lowering the charge of LPS thus inhibiting the interaction between the positively charged colistin with the negatively charged LPS. Complete loss of LPS is reported in A. baumanii
Spectrum of activity: Aerobic GNB except Proteus, Providencia, Morganella, Burkholderia, Serratia, Aeromonas etc.
Weight, Renal function- creatinine, Drug levels
Dose related nephrotoxicity; Dose related neurotoxicity – neuromuscular blockade (worse if aminoglycosides used concurrently)

questions.question: Colistin.

parts.text: What is colistin's mechanism of action?
Name a genetic mutation for resistance against colistin.
Describe how this mutation confers resistance exactly.

parts_raw.text: What is colistin's mechanism of action?
Name a genetic mutation for resistance against colistin.
Describe how this mutation confers resistance exactly.

questions.model_answer: a) Colistin is a cationic cyclic polypeptide that binds electrostatically to the anionic lipid A/phosphate groups of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and phospholipids in the gram-negative outer membrane, competitively displacing divalent cations (Ca2+/Mg2+); this disrupts membrane integrity, increases permeability, and causes leakage of intracellular contents and cell death (it also binds and neutralizes lipid A endotoxin). b) Chromosomal mutation/activation of the two-component regulatory systems pmrAB or phoPQ (in Klebsiella pneumoniae, inactivation of the negative regulator mgrB). c) These mutations upregulate enzymes that covalently modify lipid A by adding cationic groups (phosphoethanolamine and/or 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose), which reduces the net negative charge of the outer membrane, weakening the electrostatic binding of the positively charged colistin so it can no longer bind and disrupt the membrane.
questions.beyond_mandell: Colistin MOA and chromosomal resistance mechanisms (pmrAB/phoPQ/mgrB, lipid A modification) are not in the pp. 407-409 slice; answered from the Mandell polymyxins resistance section and established knowledge.

parts_raw.text: What is the mechanism of action (1)

questions.model_answer: a) Colistin binds electrostatically to the anionic lipid A of LPS and to phospholipids in the gram-negative outer membrane, acting as a cationic detergent that displaces Ca2+/Mg2+, disrupts the membrane, and causes leakage of intracellular components and cell death. b) mcr-1 (plasmid-borne, horizontally transferable mobile colistin resistance gene). c) mcr-1 encodes a phosphoethanolamine transferase that adds phosphoethanolamine to lipid A, reducing the net negative charge of the outer membrane; colistin can then no longer bind, so the organism survives and continues to grow despite the drug.
questions.beyond_mandell: MOA and mcr-1 mechanism are not in the pp. 407-409 slice; answered from the Mandell resistance section and Liu et al. (Lancet Infect Dis 2016, the mcr-1 reference cited on p. 409).

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Binds to LPS and phospholipids in outer membrane of gram negative bacteria, acts as cationic detergent (displaces Ca/Mg on LPS), damages cell membrane causing leakage of intracellular components. Gene: mcr-1 plasmid (horizontal transfer, mobile colistin resistant gene; note intrinsic resistance in Proteus/Serratia via LPS modification). Resistance mechanism: target modification encodes phosphatidylethanolamine - enzymatic site modification of Lipid A so colistin does not bind.

questions.model_answer: (1) Nitrofurantoin (2) Polymyxins (colistin/polymyxin B) (3) Tigecycline. (Proteus spp. and Providencia spp. are intrinsically resistant to all three despite their general gram-negative activity.)

questions.model_answer: a) Colistin penetrates the outer membrane and interacts electrostatically (via its polycationic groups) with the anionic lipid A of LPS and membrane phospholipids, competitively displacing divalent cations (Ca2+/Mg2+), disrupting membrane permeability and causing cell death; it also binds lipid A and neutralizes endotoxin. b) mcr-1 (mobilized colistin resistance-1; also mcr-2/mcr-3 with similar mechanism). c) Lipid A of LPS: mcr-1 encodes a phosphoethanolamine transferase that transfers a phosphoethanolamine residue onto lipid A, reducing its negative charge so colistin can no longer bind at its target site.
questions.beyond_mandell: MOA and mcr-1/lipid A target are not in the pp. 407-409 slice; answered from the Mandell resistance section and established knowledge.

cohort_answer.text: a) Penetrates outer cell membranes, interacts electrostatically with phospholipids (polycationic, hydrophobic/lipophilic moieties); interacts with cytoplasmic membrane changing permeability, disrupts membranes via competitive displacement of divalent cations; binds lipid A of LPS, blocking endotoxin effects (animal studies). b/c) MCR-1 (Mobilized Colistin Resistance-1) - target modification; gene encodes phosphatidylethanolamine transferase which transfers phosphatidylethanolamine residue to lipid A of gram negative cell membrane (lipid A is target binding site for colistin); also MCR-2 and 3 (similar mechanism).
